Strong skill. The name matches the folder. The description is in the third person and says both what the skill does and when to use it. The documentation matches download.py: tag idempotency through release-tag.txt, falling back past a latest release that has no index asset, refusing an asset with no digest before downloading it, the SHA-256 check, the size check against a short download, safe tar extraction, and a staged swap that restores the old index or names the .old folder. Errors print a [FAIL] line and exit non-zero. A declined or non-interactive overwrite prompt exits 1 and tells you to rerun with --force. Skipping the P: drive preflight is allowed, because dayz-conventions.md says this skill never touches P:. I ran py -m pytest -q and all 55 tests passed. Three concrete defects remain. (1) fetch_json catches only network errors (OSError and HTTPError). If a captive portal, proxy login page or GitHub outage page answers with HTTP 200 and HTML, json.loads raises a JSONDecodeError that nothing catches, so the user gets a Python traceback instead of the documented [FAIL] network message. (2) The skill checks only that the archive has a dayz-search-index/ or dayz-rag-index/ folder. It never checks that lancedb/ or manifest.json is inside before swapping out the user's working index and deleting it. A release tarball with that folder empty or partly packed would replace a good index with a broken one and still print Done. (3) In SKILL.md, the bullet 'The download lands in a temp folder... restored if the final swap fails' sits under 'Upgrading an existing index (agents)', after the agent instructions, instead of under Idempotency or Integrity checks. That makes the agent section harder to read.

The script prints a clear [FAIL] line and exits 1 on every failure path, and gates on /dayz-preflight. The destructive rebuild only runs with --full and rolls back on failure. py -m pytest -q passed all 88 tests in 0.64s, and they cover the chunkers, batch packing, retry, checkpoint, tier prompt and rollback. Concrete defects remain. (1) --status and the build disagree about a half-removed index. If lancedb/chunks.lance exists but manifest.json does not, --status prints 'No index. Run: python index.py --full' and exits 1. Running without --full then refuses with 'An index already exists'. The user gets two contradictory answers in a row. (2) The recovery hints in index.py (lines 1053 and 1061) tell the user to run 'python index.py --full' and 'python index.py --status' as bare relative commands. Those fail from the repo root, which is where the skill tells you to run from. The status hint also has no [FAIL] prefix. (3) The rollback tests use a fake LanceDB (_FakeDb and _FakeTable). No test exercises the real lancedb table_names, checkout or restore, so the riskiest recovery path is only verified against a mock. That matters because requirements.txt allows any lancedb at 0.10.0 or later, with no upper bound. (4) Ctrl+C at the 'Continue? [y/N]' free-tier prompt is not caught, so the user gets a raw traceback instead of one [FAIL] line. The embed and write phases do catch Ctrl+C.

The name matches the folder, and the description is third person and says both what the skill does and when to use it. The script runs the preflight check first, exits non-zero with a clear [FAIL] line on every failure path, refuses to import a .reg that writes outside HKEY_CURRENT_USER, and refuses while Object Builder is running or when tasklist cannot tell. Before any import over an existing key it backs the key up with reg export, it asks for confirmation (or needs --yes) before a forced reset, and it restores the backup on its own if the import fails. All 58 tests pass (py -m pytest -q, 0.46s). They cover the import and restore paths, the backup and delete ordering, the confirmation prompt, the foreign-key check and preference write failures. One defect is left that a user would hit: --force on a partial tree does not reset. If the Object Builder key exists but its CConfig subkey is missing, line 345 of setup.py takes the merge branch even with --force. So there is no reg delete and no confirmation, and the stale MainFrame-* panel layouts the user ran --force to clear are kept. SKILL.md says the opposite: step 5 says --force deletes the key, and How to run calls --force a reset to factory defaults. No test runs --force against a partial tree. Two smaller points: SKILL.md is long and dense (one 'How to run' paragraph packs the project-root resolution order, the --yes rule and the restore behaviour together), and the real reg import, export and delete commands are only tested with mocked subprocess calls.

The name matches the folder. The description is in the third person and says what the skill does and when to use it. SKILL.md matches add_scaffold.py closely: piece order, junction kept out of 'all', each [OK]/[SKIP]/[WARN]/[FAIL] line, the rule that a single skipped or wrong piece exits 1, the author being resolved before anything is written, and the name being checked before preflight. A read-only or locked file (for example a OneDrive-synced or read-only clone) crashes with a raw PermissionError traceback, and earlier pieces are left half-written with no summary line.

The skill is solid. Well built overall. The name matches the folder, and the description is third person and says what the skill does and when to use it. The SKILL.md matches the script: the exit codes 0, 1 and 2, the first-line verdict, the --json stdout rule, the refusal of a partly unpacked snapshot with --accept to override it, the atomic save through a .tmp file, and skipping unreadable snapshots with a note. The script is readable, raises GuardError with clear messages and exits non-zero on failure. dayz-conventions.md line 27 documents the preflight exception, and the script checks P:\scripts and P:\DZ itself. It deletes nothing, and a mistyped mod name or an empty workspace is caught before anything is saved. All 55 tests pass (py -m pytest -q took 1.70s). A real snapshot of P:\ worked: 6903 script classes and 27701 config classes in about 9s, exit 0. Two concrete defects remain. (1) False positives: method signatures keep parameter names. I confirmed that parse_method('void OnX(int a, float b = 1)') gives 'void OnX(int a, float b)' while 'void OnX(int c, float d)' gives a different string. So when vanilla only renames a parameter, which DayZ updates often do, every mod override of that method is flagged override-changed and FAIL is reported for code that still compiles. (2) A false negative: check_mod only looks at methods marked `override`. When an update adds a vanilla method whose name matches a method the mod already declares without `override`, the guard reports PASS, but the mod no longer compiles (Enforce requires `override` there). The Limits section does not mention this case. A smaller issue: the newest snapshot is chosen by file-name sort, not by the snapshot's `created` field. A name that sorts later, such as one saved under a wrong clock, stays the baseline. My run showed this: a stray 20991231-000000.json in the store was picked first, and was only skipped because it happened to be corrupt.

The name matches the folder, and the description is in the third person and says both what the skill does and when to use it. One concrete defect remains, and I reproduced it: gate_on_template_mismatch (add_server.py line 161) compares the config's template = line case-sensitively, while gate_on_mission_source and the junction cleanup use casefold. So an instance created with --map dayzoffline.enoch and rerun with --map dayzOffline.enoch is refused with "set up for mission template 'dayzoffline.enoch', not 'dayzOffline.enoch'", although Windows treats them as the same folder. Adding --refresh-mission does not help; the user has to hand-edit serverDZ.cfg. A smaller issue: SKILL.md is very long (step 5 alone is a dense paragraph), which goes against the guidance to keep a skill concise.

The file is mostly well built. The description is in the third person with a realistic example, Skill and an explicit Agent allowlist cover the body, the Report section names the user, and the gate flags, triage fields and other skill flags it cites all check out against the skill files (--accept/--replace-failed/--yes, owner_agent and fingerprint, /dayz-health record <ModName> review from standard input, /dayz-new-mod --author with the cached .claude/local-memory/dayz-author.txt, /dayz-add-server --map, /dayz-recipe weapon|vest|craftable). Two defects are concrete. (1) It breaks the team flow. dayz-mod-architect.md line 31 tells the orchestrator to run `/dayz-gate behavior <ModName> --prepare-only` with the plan's --deps and --server once the mod and server are set up, before the first wave, and to send errors naming behavior-checks.json back to the architect. The orchestrator has no such step. A malformed checks file is therefore found only after a full wave has been built and the build and in-game gates have passed, which costs one of the three gate rounds and a game launch. (2) Line 13 says the Agent list must include every agent the leads start 'because their subagents inherit it'. The current subagent spec says Agent(type) allowlists apply only to the agent running as the main thread, that type lists inside a subagent definition are ignored, and that nesting is limited by spawn depth, not by an inherited allowlist. The roughly 50-entry tools line (every worker listed under both its bare and agentic-z: name) rests on an unsupported rationale, and a maintainer who trusts it will keep growing that line. Minor point: steps 5 and 6 are dense and repeat routing detail that already lives in skills/dayz-gate/SKILL.md and triage.md.

A strong skill with two real bugs left. The name matches the folder. The description is third person and says both what the skill does and when to use it. SKILL.md matches the script closely: preflight runs first, backups are timestamped, there is a dry run in every mode, only the changed <type> blocks are rewritten, encoding and line endings are kept, and failures print a [FAIL] line and exit non-zero. `py -m pytest -q` passed 123 tests in 1.13s, and they cover the risky logic: block-by-block patching, CRLF, ISO-8859-1 and UTF-16 files, case-insensitive matching, merge validation and write or backup failures. Tested by hand on a copy of the vanilla chernarusplus types.xml, two bugs showed up. (1) Adding a new entry with a repeated flag (`MyItem --usage Military --usage Military`) writes `<usage name="Military"/>` twice, while updating an existing entry removes the duplicate. (2) A class name with spaces at either end gets past every check. A merge chunk with `<type name=" AKM ">` reports `Added <type name=" AKM ">` next to the existing AKM instead of replacing it. Single-entry mode has the same gap, because the `non_blank` check and `find_type` never strip spaces. The result is a dead entry the Central Economy matches to no class, and the file then looks like it lists AKM twice. Smaller gap: `--remove` combined with field flags quietly ignores them (as documented) with no warning.

The name matches the folder, the description is in third person and says both what it does and when to use it, and the installer is careful: it refuses on invalid JSON, takes a numbered backup that never overwrites an older one, records and restores the user's previous status line, exits 1 with a clear message when no project is found, and correctly skips the preflight gate. All 37 tests passed. One concrete defect: SKILL.md says the 'mod ?' segment appears when .claude\local-memory\dayz-init-state.json is broken, and tells the user to fix that file. In practice dayz-init/state.py read_state() swallows JSONDecodeError and returns an empty dict, so a file with invalid JSON shows 'no active mod'. I reproduced this: a state file containing '{broken' printed 'P: mounted | no active mod | ...'. Only non-JSON bytes or a null last_intent produce 'mod ?'. A user whose state file is corrupt sees a normal-looking 'no active mod' and is never pointed at the real fault. No test covers a state file with invalid JSON.

Mostly solid. The name matches the folder. The description is in the third person and says what the skill does and when to use it. The script runs preflight first, refuses read-only or already-split files before touching anything, makes timestamped backups, checks that the split files hold the same number of type entries as the original, and restores everything automatically on failure, and it exits 1 when it fails. All 22 tests pass. I also ran it end to end on a scratch copy of the vanilla Chernarus files from P:\, and it split all 2382 entries into 19 files, rewrote cfgeconomycore.xml to point at db/types and emptied types.xml. Four problems a user would actually hit. (1) The vendored splitter logs one INFO line per type, so a vanilla run prints 2421 lines; the skill does not hide or summarise them, which floods an agent's context and buries the result lines. (2) cfgeconomycore.xml loses all its comments, including vanilla's notes on act="character" and act="car" plus one comment per rootclass. The wrapper already copies lost ce blocks back from the backup but does nothing for comments, and the SKILL.md only tells the user to compare against the backup. (3) The SKILL.md sample output says 14 non-empty category files, but vanilla gives 19. Step 5 also calls its key claim (that ce folder paths are relative to the mission root) unverified, even though the whole fix depends on it. (4) The tests use a 4-entry fixture with no comments. Nothing tests vanilla-shaped input, comment loss, or a cfgeconomycore.xml without classes or defaults, where the upstream formatter crashes and falls back to one ce block per file.

The skill's name matches its folder. The description is in the third person and says both what the skill does and when to use it. SKILL.md matches ask.py closely: the flags, the top-k range of 1 to 25, the distance cutoff of 1.15, the 60-line excerpt cap and the EVIDENCE/NONE/ERROR exit codes 0/1/2 all agree. Live runs confirmed the error paths: an empty question, a question made only of common words and --top-k 30 each give ERROR with exit 2, a nonsense question gives NONE with exit 1, and --grep returns grep citations. The skill is read-only, checks that P:\ is mounted itself, and nothing in it needs a backup or confirmation guard. Running py -m pytest -q gives 44 passed. The tests cover hit checking (verified, moved and changed), off-topic dropping, re-citing long class hits, grep ranking, falling back to grep, and the CLI exit codes. The concrete defect: SKILL.md's own example question ('what does the food config set for spoil time', run here with --file-type cpp) returns EVIDENCE with 4 citations via RAG. All 4 are empty stubs from P:\dz\gear\food\config.cpp: FoodAnimationSources at lines 170-208, and FruitStageTransitions, MushroomsStageTransitions and MeatStageTransitions, each just 'class X: BaseFoodStageTransitions {};'. They survive only because the generic term 'food' appears in a class name, and none says anything about spoil time. The name matches the folder, the description is third person and says what it does and when to use it, and model invocation is disabled for a destructive skill. This is a strong skill. The name matches the folder. The description is in the third person and says what the skill does and when to use it. Preflight runs first, as the repo rules require, and the mod name is validated before anything touches the disk. Destructive steps are guarded: an ownership marker protects the deploy folder, and --clean is refused when Addons holds other PBOs or .bisign files. I confirmed three defects. (1) If $PBOPREFIX$ is saved as UTF-16 (Notepad's 'Unicode' option), gate_on_prefix crashes with a raw UnicodeDecodeError traceback instead of a [FAIL] line and a hint. The name matches the folder. The description is third person and says what the skill does and when to use it. SKILL.md matches the script closely: the steps, flags and refusals all line up. Preflight runs first (build_imageset.py:533, and a test checks it). Errors are clear with exit 1, conversion goes through a staging folder so failures stay atomic, dry run is supported, and --prune is opt-in. All 73 tests pass (py -m pytest -q, 0.78s). One concrete gap remains: the stale-output cleanup in remove_stale_outputs (build_imageset.py:233-267) deletes any file in gui/imagesets/ whose name matches <set> or <set>_<digits>. It does not first run the looks_generated() check that orphan pruning uses, and it runs without --prune. Example: a mod has a set folder `hud`, and its old set folder `hud_2024` has been deleted. A normal run silently deletes hud_2024.imageset and hud_2024.paa as 'stale', even though SKILL.md says orphans are only deleted with --prune. A locked final file, for example one held open by Workbench, makes os.replace in promote_staged (line 229) raise a raw traceback partway through moving files, which can leave the set half-replaced.

The skill is in good shape. Its name matches the folder, the description is third person and says both what it does and when to use it, the SKILL.md matches bootstrap.py closely, preflight runs first, the script stops only the processes it started, Ctrl+C cleanup is handled, every edited file gets a .bak backup first, and all 70 tests pass (py -m pytest -q: 70 passed in 0.66s). The defect a user would hit is in edit_permissions (bootstrap.py lines 271-283): it calls grant_admin_role, which writes "admin" into Players/<id>.json, before it checks that Permissions/<id>.txt exists. If COT never writes the perms file within the 15-second wait, the run exits 1 with the JSON already granted and the perms file not flipped, which is exactly the half-applied grant the code comment says it avoids. A rerun with --skip-pass1 then passes, because admin_players only checks the JSON role, and relaunches with that half grant. The test test_edit_permissions_fails_when_perms_file_missing checks only the False return value and never asserts that the JSON was left alone, so the tests miss this. Smaller issues: flip_zeros_to_twos does not catch UnicodeDecodeError or OSError, so a perms file that is not UTF-8 crashes with a traceback after the JSON was already edited. There is also no --dry-run, although /dayz-launch-test, whose launch contract this skill reuses, has one.

Strong skill. The name matches the folder. The description is third person and says both what the skill does and when to use it. SKILL.md matches update.py on every flag, exit code, refuse rule, the status table and the template path list. The 20-second SessionStart hook in .claude/settings.json and the gitignored baseline and lock files are both as documented. Errors are clear and the exit codes are right. Destructive steps are guarded by a y/N prompt (--yes skips it), --dry-run, a dirty-tree gate, a check for a merge or rebase in progress, an atomic PID lock with stale-lock takeover, and a commit limited to the applied paths. `py -m pytest -q` passes all 132 tests in 47 seconds. Two concrete defects remain, both on large drift. (1) compute_drift starts about three git processes for every candidate file (two rev-parse calls plus hash-object). I measured about 56 ms per git call on this machine, so a clone a few hundred template files behind upstream takes longer than the hook's 20-second timeout. The hook is then killed and prints nothing, so users who are furthest behind never see the nudge. (2) stage_and_commit passes every applied path on the command line to both git add and git commit --only. A large first update (the repo tracks over 500 template files) can go past the Windows command-line limit of about 32,000 characters. The commit then fails and leaves the files staged with the baseline not moved. No test covers either case.

The skill meets the structural rules. The name matches the folder. The description is in the third person and says both what the skill does and when to use it. The name matches the folder, and the description is third person and says both what the skill does and when to use it. The script is readable and matches SKILL.md: its exit codes are 0 for PASS, 1 for FLAG, 2 for ERROR and 3 for UNCHECKED, and I confirmed that a missing folder and a bad --ratio each print ERROR and exit 2. It is read-only and listed as an exception to the preflight gate in dayz-conventions.md, so it has no destructive steps that need guarding. (1) The 'firearm rounds' ammo family is impure. On the real P:\DZ, the 21 lethal peers include Bullet_40mm_Base, Bullet_40mm_ChemGas (a grenade-launcher gas round) and Dart_Syringe. SKILL.md also says these 21 run 'from Bullet_22 ... to Bullet_308Win', which hides this. (2) The text report contradicts itself. A user sees two 'not compared' lines but only one item missing from the count.

The name matches the folder. The description is in the third person and says both what the skill does and when to use it. SKILL.md matches deploy.py step for step: name check first, then project cache, preflight, P:\Mods junction, bundle check, ownership marker gate, linker-name refusal, newer-file guard, additive copy, stale and unsigned warnings, marker. Errors are clear [FAIL] lines with hints and every failure exits non-zero. Overwrites are guarded by --dry-run and a newer-file refusal, and --force is documented as having no backup. `py -m pytest -q` on the skill passes all 43 tests, which cover the copy decisions, the mtime tolerance, the ownership gate, linker collisions, stale files, dry run, locked files and an unwritable marker. One defect remains. deploy.py copies with shutil.copy2 straight onto the destination and does not clean up after a failure partway through a file. That happens on Ctrl+C during a large PBO (KeyboardInterrupt is not caught, so no marker is written either) or when the disk fills. The truncated file keeps the current time as its modified time, so on the rerun deployed_is_newer() treats it as a newer build and the deploy refuses with "Deployed file(s) are newer than the bundle copy". The user can only get past it with --force, the flag SKILL.md says not to pass by default. That contradicts SKILL.md step 7, which says the rerun simply picks up where it left off.

The name matches the folder, and the description is third person with a clear 'Use when'. The script is readable, its error messages give the next step, and every refusal exits non-zero through sys.exit. It runs the Workshop and no-TTY checks first, then gates on preflight before touching anything, as the rules require. The destructive paths are guarded: it refuses to clobber an existing folder, rolls back the workspace link if the P: junction fails, deletes a clone this run made when a later step refuses, and never deletes a reused clone. All 87 tests pass under py -m pytest -q in 1.5s, and they cover the risky logic: UNC paths, paths inside workspace/, null stdin, the '..' subfolder escape, rollback, clone cleanup and slash branches. Three concrete defects remain. (1) The Output example in SKILL.md shows the prompt 'Path to existing mod folder:', but the script prints 'Path or GitHub link:' (import_mod.py line 196), so the docs do not match the script. (2) Pressing Ctrl+C during a long git clone into workspace/<Name> skips remove_clone, because only a non-zero git return code triggers cleanup. The half-cloned folder stays behind. The next run then refuses with 'already exists', and the cleanup it points to, /dayz-clean-workspace, refuses any folder that holds .git, so the user has to delete it by hand. (3) If git ls-remote fails (offline or bad credentials), resolve_branch falls back to the first path segment. A tree link to a branch such as feature/x is then cloned as branch 'feature' with subfolder 'x'. The clone fails, and the git error does not say that the branch was guessed. No test covers a P: junction failure on the repo-link clone path (import_from_git), and none covers an interrupted clone.

The skill is in good shape. The name matches the folder, the description is third-person and says what it does and when to use it, and the script is read-only with clear errors. Exit codes are as documented: an unknown flag and a missing folder both gave ERROR with exit 2, a default run gave PARTIAL with exit 0, and a collision gave FAIL with exit 1. It handles a missing P:\ cleanly, and running py -m pytest -q gave 40 passed. One real defect: SKILL.md says the check 'takes about a second', and that holds against packed mods (0.46 s for the default run, 13 s for --all). But when your mod and an unpacked mod both define the same config class, the lazy vanilla lookup in Vanilla.config_class walks every config.cpp under P:\DZ. I ran `py -m pytest -q` on the skill: 51 tests passed in 0.35s. Those tests cover the risky logic: the two flags excluding each other, relative `--file` lookup order and its error message, the `--mod` name rule and the reserved P: folders, recursive .p3d search with the 20-item cap, preflight running before the target is resolved, the registry check, refusing a second instance, a tasklist failure, and a process that exits straight away. The name matches the folder. The description is third person and says both what the skill does and when to use it. `launch.py` matches what SKILL.md describes: preflight, then resolve, find the exe, check the registry, check for a running instance, spawn detached, then a one-second exit check. Failures use [FAIL] lines, go to stderr and exit non-zero, and nothing is destructive. Four concrete defects remain. (1) Any early exit makes the script tell the user to run `/dayz-setup-objectbuilder --force`. That command resets Object Builder to factory defaults and deletes custom layouts; a backup is made, but a missing DLL or a broken install leads the user into a pointless reset. (2) The invalid-mod-name message hardcodes 'max 64 chars' and the allowed characters, while the check itself uses NAME_PATTERN loaded from new_mod.py, so the message goes stale if that rule changes. (3) The script loads setup.py, the workbench launch.py and new_mod.py when it starts. If one is missing or renamed, the user gets a raw Python traceback instead of a clear [FAIL] line. (4) SKILL.md is longer than it needs to be: 'Flag rules' and 'Do not' repeat most of 'What it does', including the project-root search order, which goes against the best practice of keeping skills concise.

Overall this skill is strong. The name matches the folder. The description is in the third person and says what the skill checks and when to use it. Every rule in SKILL.md exists in lint.py and has a lint-<rule> entry in known-errors.json. Output follows a strict contract: the verdict comes first, and the exit code is 0 for PASS, 1 for FAIL and 2 for ERROR; argparse errors also come back as ERROR with exit 2. A path passed as the mod name is refused. The skill is read-only, so it needs no backup or dry run. py -m pytest -q passed all 87 tests in 1.49s. A real run took 0.67s and caught a modded class with extends, missing model and texture files, and a typo in a DZ_ requiredAddons name. I confirmed two defects. (1) A false p-link error for every mod set up by /dayz-import-mod when it is linted with --mod-dir. main() calls args.mod_dir.resolve(), which follows the workspace junction to the external source folder. The P:\<Mod> link points at workspace\<Mod>, as import_mod.link_source creates it, so check_link's paths_equal(target, mod_dir) does not match. I reproduced this with real junctions: the run reported 'P:\TestMod points at ...\ws\TestMod, not at ...\TestMod', and a FAIL from the lint also fails the build. Linting by <ModName> does not hit this, because that path is not resolved. No test covers the junction case. (2) The modded-class-extends check removes comments with a regex that does not know about strings. If a string contains '/*', for example "scripts/*", and a later string contains '*/', the code between them is removed. A 'modded class PlayerBase extends PlayerBase' placed there was not reported. That is a missed error, not a false alarm.

A strong skill overall. The name matches the folder, the description is in the third person and says both what it does and when to use it, the script is readable and exits 2 with a clear ERROR line, it correctly skips preflight because it never touches P:\, and all 71 tests pass (py -m pytest -q, 0.68s). One documented behaviour fails in real use, though. SKILL.md says a UTF-8 byte order mark is fine and that FILE can be left out so the report comes from standard input. But health.py reads sys.stdin without setting its encoding, and on Windows a piped stdin is read as cp1252. I confirmed this. Piping a review that starts with a BOM into `health.py record <Mod> review` returns 'ERROR: a review report starts with a PASS or FAIL line' with exit 2, because the BOM arrives as the three characters 'ï»¿' and text.removeprefix('\ufeff') never matches. The same report passed as FILE parses fine. Piped UTF-8 text without a BOM, such as an em dash in a finding, is read as cp1252 too, so it would be stored and shown garbled on the page (inferred from the encoding, not run). The tests miss this because they pass io.StringIO objects that are already decoded, so the real stdin path is never tested. Smaller issues: a JSON review with verdict FAIL and no findings is accepted, while the text form refuses it. A build result repeats its lint failures, and because duplicates are kept in gate order (build first), open lint findings show under 'Build' rather than 'Lint'. The argument-hint and 'How to run' section leave out the 'show' subcommand that the script's docstring and parser accept.

Mostly solid. The name matches the folder, and the description is in the third person and says both what the skill does and when to use it, pointing to the sibling skills for the other cases. A partial scaffold is rolled back if a step fails or Ctrl+C is pressed. The only destructive step removes a stale link, and only when that link points at the exact workspace folder being created. 'py -m pytest -q' ran 58 tests and all passed. I ran the gproj injection against the real DayZ Tools dayz.gproj: all three module paths and both filesystem mounts went in cleanly. One concrete defect remains. The project folder is resolved in this order: CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR, then a cache above the working directory, then the clone holding the script (only if that clone already has a cache), and finally the working directory. So if the shell starts outside the repo (as this harness's shells do), the mod is created at <working directory>/workspace/<ModName>, a P:\ junction is made to it, and the /dayz-init project cache points at that wrong folder. Nothing warns about this. A smaller issue: if dayz-init-state.json is corrupt, read_state silently returns an empty dict, and sync_project_cache then overwrites the file, erasing every other key without a warning.

I read every file in the skill folder and ran its four test files: 294 passed. Defect 1: gate.py:748 sets the deadline when the launch starts and never moves it, and gate.py:770 checks it even after the ready line has appeared. I ran watch_session with a fake clock: the client joined at 290 s with a 300 s timeout, and the gate returned the failure "client never reached the mission within 300 s" although it had found the ready line. Because of this, the default --done-timeout of 600 that SKILL.md:37 describes as time after the client joins can never be reached, and a late join or a long visual or behavior run gets a false FAIL. The sources the entry itself cites, api_game.md and troubleshooting.md, say that reading is unsettled, and they also advise retrying with no earlier join still running. The fix is to mark the code unsettled here as well and add that retry step.
